title: Claude Fable 5.1 helped me build my Bigfoot game's first "you are a Bigfoot" mechanic: tree-kicking, plus see-through trees to watch it happen
author: thezirHaze
selftext:
Solo dev on LittleBigFoot, a cozy stealth adventure where you're a young LittleBigfoot raised by a park ranger. Almost everything the player does (cooking, fishing, looting) is a human activity done in disguise. This week I shipped the first verb that only a Bigfoot can do: kick a fruit tree and 1–2 apples shake loose onto the ground.

The interesting problem wasn't the kick. It was seeing it. The apple tree's canopy sits between the camera and the player, so the payoff landed on ground you couldn't see. The naive fix is an occlusion cutout keyword on the materials, but the fruit and trunk sit on materials shared by 3,000+ and 1,300+ renderers in the scene, and a fragment `clip()` costs early-Z on *every* renderer wearing the material, so flipping the keyword on the shared assets would tax a third of the park to open a hole in one tree. The shipped solution: at runtime, each renderer that should participate gets swapped onto an otherwise-identical material variant that carries the keyword. Nothing else pays.

Favorite iteration moment: the cutout was cutting holes in apples *on the ground*. Hanging fruit and dropped fruit are the same mesh on the same material, so "which apples go transparent" can't live on the asset at all. It has to be decided at runtime by who owns the apple. One correction from me, and the model restructured around ownership instead of asset.

Clip below. Happy to share how I structure the sessions if anyone's curious.

comments.author: HeadacheOwner
comments.body: Can I ask how you have handled the graphics? Looks good!

replies.author: thezirHaze
replies.body:
Thanks! It is flat colour rather than flat shading, and it is basically one texture doing all the work.

Every surface in the game samples a single 256x256 palette atlas, an 8x8 grid of 32px cells, with about 44 colours in use. The project has no UV unwrapping. Each face's UVs collapse to a single point at the centre of whichever cell it should be, so UV area is literally zero and texel density, seams, and stretching stop existing as problems. Import is point filter, no mips, no compression, because with UVs sitting at cell centres, bilinear filtering would sample the neighbouring cells and tint everything with colours I never picked.

Geometry stays smooth-shaded, not faceted. The goal is a matte painted surface with a soft gradient across it rather than visible polygons.

The part that actually sells it, though, is a custom URP shader. It does real aerial perspective: colour shifts toward a pale mist tone with distance, scaled to the park's longest sightline rather than a fixed metre value, plus a subtle vertical gradient from ground to canopy. Without that, flat colour reads as a flat illustration. With it, you get depth across the whole park. Same shader handles the vertex sway on foliage and the see-through cutout in the clip.

Cheap to run and very fast to author, which matters a lot solo.
